### Generation 1
Your analysis then: The only evidence is the constant construction with R=2/3. A Gaussian f gives R=1/sqrt(2)=0.7071, so the first test should be the Gaussian family. Beyond that, the most promising line is direct shape optimization of step heights using the exact analytic gradient of R, with positivity via log-heights and multi-start/continuation. A genuinely different branch is to design f so that f*f approximates a flat-top target by least squares, since a rectangle autoconvolution would have R near 1; this tests whether flat-target deconvolution accesses shapes the direct R gradient misses.

### Generation 2
Your analysis then: The evidence is clear: fitting f so f*f approximates a flat-top target (p0003, 0.8494) beats direct R optimization from a generic start (p0006, 0.8197) and all hill-climbing. The current best is only N=300 and used a coarse trapezoid target grid, so the likely gains are (i) higher resolution direct-R polishing from that shape with p0006's exact gradient, (ii) richer flat-top target profiles, and (iii) a genuinely different spectral projection for inverting the autoconvolution target. I am betting the flat-top principle is right but under-explored at high N and with better target geometry.

### Generation 3
Your analysis then: p0012 (0.8629) shows direct-R polish at high N beats target fitting (p0013/p0011 ~0.856) and that the winning f*f is asymmetric: its max sits at 0.342 of the support with a broad plateau (28% of knots within 5%). Two levers follow: (i) p0012 used a fixed N=1500, while p0009/p0010 showed multi-resolution ladders help; (ii) the off-centre maximum suggests deliberate asymmetry, which no target-fitting run ever tried (all were symmetric). I bet on a resolution ladder, on asymmetric seeding of the direct-R polish, and on flattening p0012's own f*f plateau as a re-inversion target.

### Generation 4
Your analysis then: p0018 (0.8661) is the strongest; its gain came from N=3000 plus skew seeds, but it still has only 22% of f*f knots within 1% of the max, so plateau ripple remains. p0015's ladder did not beat it alone, and p0019's flattening fit underperformed, suggesting local optima/nonsmooth max and basin choice matter. I bet on (1) a resolution sweep around 3000, (2) softmax smoothing of the max to flatten the plateau, and (3) combining p0015's ladder basin with p0018's skew seeds.

### Generation 5
Your analysis then: p0025's softmax annealing on the max knot gave the biggest jump since the flat-top fit (+0.0119 to 0.8780), and it left 28% of f*f knots within 0.1% of max — the plateau is nearly flat but still narrow. The nonsmooth-max smoothing is the right lever. I bet on (1) pushing the anneal far deeper in tau with a repeated schedule, (2) the same anneal on a finer grid so fine structure is resolvable, and (3) a genuinely different smoothing: a locally window-averaged max that penalizes ripple at a fixed length scale rather than pointwise spikes.

### Generation 6
Your analysis then: Gains are now tiny (+0.0009): p0030's deep softmax reached 31% of knots within 0.1% of max, and finer grids (p0031, p0027) do not help, so resolution and tau-depth are near-saturated. The remaining loss is either (i) the exponential softmax weighting being the wrong smoothing family, (ii) the nonsmooth max still fixing a cap the plateau cannot pull up against, or (iii) ripple-scale local optima trapping the fine-grid basin. I bet on replacing the smoothing with a scale-free power mean, on a hard-cap smooth-penalty formulation that pushes every plateau knot to the same ceiling, and on a coarse-grid round-trip to escape fine-scale traps.
